matches.rationale: GT1 describes inflated sample efficiency metrics in Figure 6(b) that are inconsistent with the learning curves in Figure 6(a). Finding 5 identifies a different inconsistency: the text claims '20-67%' reduction but the table shows 28.7-82.3%. These are distinct issues about different aspects of the data reporting.

Both identify the same sign error in the f^{return} target function in Section 3.1. GT2 describes the advantage weighting sign error and its contradiction with the stated goal. Finding 3 explicitly identifies the negative sign in the formula and explains how maximizing it would decrease (not increase) probability of better-than-average actions.

GT3 concerns the failure to disclose which specific p value was used for each environment in the main results, creating unfair comparison. None of the findings address this selective reporting of hyperparameter choices or the p-value selection issue.

Both identify overclaiming in the abstract. GT4 notes the abstract claims IIF 'eliminates sample inefficiency' and 'completely solves training instability' while results show only partial improvements. Finding 8 directly quotes the abstract's claim of 'completely eliminates sample inefficiency' and contrasts it with the 20-67% (or 82.3%) partial reduction reported in results.

GT5 concerns fabricated or premature citations to 'Cheng et al., 2025' and 'Deng et al., 2025' in Section 6. Finding 7 identifies a fabricated 'Kumar et al., 2024' citation in the Introduction, and Finding 9 identifies a missing 'Williams, 1992' citation. These are different citations in different sections.

GT6 concerns the omission of ethical considerations and failure mode discussion in safety-critical LLM applications (Section 5.3 and Section 7). None of the findings address ethical integrity, societal impact, or dual-use concerns.

GT7 concerns rhetorical exaggeration and marketing-style language in the Introduction ('completely solves,' 'unprecedented,' 'revolutionary breakthrough'). While Finding 8 identifies overclaiming, it focuses on the abstract's specific technical claims rather than the rhetorical tone issue GT7 describes.

Both identify the contradiction about whether the reference policy is dynamic or static. GT8 notes Section 3.1 says π^{ref} = π_{θ^{(k)}} (dynamic, updated each round) while Appendix A.2 describes a 'fixed reference policy trained to convergence.' Finding 2 quotes the exact same contradiction in Section 3.1 between 'fixed, pre-trained policy' and 'dynamic reference evolves with training.'

GT9 concerns manipulation of y-axis ranges in Figure 6(a) to visually amplify differences (e.g., omitting early Acrobot rounds, using narrow MiniGrid range). None of the findings address visual encoding manipulation or selective axis scaling in the figures.

GT10 concerns asymmetric experimental design where IIF benefits from hyperparameter optimization ('various p's and report the best') while baselines use default hyperparameters. None of the findings address this unfair comparison or asymmetric tuning protocol.

GT11 concerns the claim of 'consistent improvement' despite wide confidence intervals in Appendix B.8 and contradictory evidence in Figure 11 showing performance degradation in some rounds. None of the findings address statistical uncertainty, confidence intervals, or cherry-picking of favorable interpretations.

Both identify inconsistencies in the influence score formula. GT12 notes the learning rate η_j is missing and θ_j^{(k)} is used inconsistently. Finding 4 documents three mutually inconsistent descriptions of the influence score across Section 3.1 and 5.1, including the discrepancy between the general definition (sum over steps) and implementation (single evaluation).

GT13 concerns potential selective reporting of environments, noting that negative results in appendices (difficulty-based filtering, TD error heuristics) suggest possible unreported failures. None of the findings address publication bias, selective environment reporting, or missing negative results.

GT14 concerns misattribution of the f^{return} formulation to 'REINFORCE with a baseline [Sutton and Barto, 2018, Section 13.4]' when the cited section doesn't describe this specific construction. Finding 9 identifies a missing Williams 1992 citation but doesn't address the Sutton and Barto misattribution issue.

GT15 concerns the contradiction between Section 5.1's claim of 'negligible overhead' and Table 5/Table 6 showing influence calculation takes 7-15% of per-round time (and is the second most expensive component in RLHF). None of the findings address computational overhead claims or the cost breakdown inconsistency.
